nameStory: The Artillery Plant gets its explosive name from its remarkable seed-shooting ability! When the tiny flowers are ripe, they literally fire their pollen into the air like miniature cannons, creating small puffs that look like gunpowder smoke. This dramatic display earned it the nickname "joypowder plant" in some regions.
description: Artillery Plant is a small, delicate annual with tiny leaves and almost succulent-looking light green stems. It rarely grows taller than 6-12 inches, forming low, spreading mats that make it popular as a ground cover in warmer climates. The leaves are so small they're barely noticeable, giving the plant a fine, lacy appearance from a distance. Originally from tropical regions, it's quite rare in New England and typically only survives in very protected locations.

idTips.label: Leaves
idTips.description: Extremely tiny, rounded leaves that feel slightly thick and succulent-like when gently pinched, arranged in pairs along the stems

idTips.label: Stems
idTips.description: Light green, translucent stems that look almost watery or succulent, feeling smooth and slightly squishy to the touch

idTips.label: Growth Habit
idTips.description: Forms low, spreading mats only a few inches tall, with a delicate, fine-textured appearance that looks almost moss-like from a distance

idTips.label: Flowers
idTips.description: Microscopic greenish flowers that are barely visible but may produce tiny puffs of pollen when disturbed

habitat: In New England, Artillery Plant is extremely rare and typically found only in very warm, protected locations such as heated greenhouses, conservatories, or occasionally as a temporary escape near buildings. It requires consistently warm temperatures and cannot survive New England winters outdoors.

seasonality.spring: May appear as tiny seedlings in very warm, protected locations, with pale green succulent-like stems just beginning to spread.
seasonality.summer: Reaches full size and may produce its microscopic flowers during the warmest months, forming low mats in suitable locations.
seasonality.fall: Begins to decline as temperatures drop, with stems becoming more translucent and brittle before the first frost.
seasonality.winter: Cannot survive New England winters outdoors; only persists in heated indoor environments like greenhouses.

funFact: Artillery Plant can actually shoot its pollen up to several feet through the air when the tiny flowers explode open, and if you gently blow on a mature plant or mist it with water, you might see little puffs of pollen firing off like tiny fireworks!
confusionNotes: Its tiny leaves and succulent-like stems make it unlikely to be confused with most New England plants, but in greenhouse settings it might be mistaken for baby's tears or small moss until you notice the distinctly succulent feel of the stems and the paired leaf arrangement.
contextualKnowledge: This tropical native is much more commonly seen as a houseplant or in greenhouse collections than growing wild in New England. Its various common names like "joypowder plant" and "angeloweed" reflect its popularity in warmer climates where it readily naturalizes.
compareHints: Unlike its New England relatives Canada clearweed and springs clearweed, Artillery Plant has much smaller, more succulent-feeling leaves and stems, and lacks the translucent "windows" in the stems that give other clearweeds their name. The other clearweeds also grow much taller and have a more upright, less mat-forming growth habit.

relatedSpecies.distinction: Canada clearweed is much more common than its relative springs clearweed, which prefers wetter conditions near actual springs and streams.
Springs clearweed is nearly identical to Canada clearweed in appearance and habitat, making them one of the trickiest plant pairs to distinguish in New England.
